entries.title: raddle: codeguide's woven-in successor
entries.brief: Docs regenerated once at merge time over the plan's diff, folded into Finalize's contract; the geometry and the parallel-regeneration design exist
entries.body:
From `manifest/roadmap.md` Someday.
raddle is codeguide's woven-in successor.
A parallel-regeneration design exists.
It folds into `Finalize`'s own contract rather than a separate producer, since `Shed` has no slots for it to occupy.

## Design

> **Status: Design partially exists, not scheduled.** Deprioritized — not required to land a first `loom` plan. Raddle-regeneration is folded into `Finalize`'s own contract, not a reserved phase slot of its own (see `contracts/recipes/loom-recipe.yaml`). This doc covers the parts of raddle's design settled during the vacation-time discussion, not the whole module.

## What it is

Raddle is codeguide's weaving-vocabulary successor, living in `weft`: it generates docs over the diff a plan produced, building heavily on Millhouse's `codeguide-update`, deliberately not the implementer's job — implementers, busy with code, forget the docs.
See When it runs below for when regeneration actually happens.

## Geometry — where raddle content lives

Every raddle file lives under `_lyx/raddle/` inside each worktree, mirroring that worktree's own code tree.
It is resolved by plain path lookup joined onto the anchor path, with no junction of its own and no hub-level presence at all.
It reaches the weft through the already-wired `_lyx` junction, like every other `_lyx` subtree.

`_raddle` is **not** a reserved hub name and is never junction-reached.

Raddle content is tracked `_lyx` content and therefore needs no `.lyx` mirror, per the Durable-vs-Ephemeral State Invariant.

This section records the geometry only — raddle's actual implementation, including the shadow tree's path-lookup code and any accessor, is explicitly out of scope here.

## Parallel regeneration — unlike card implementation, this is safe

Unlike webster's card implementation (which needs real worktree isolation for safe parallelism — see webster-parallel-execution.md), raddle's doc regeneration can safely run as **parallel forks**, for reasons specific to what raddle does:

1. **No per-fork git commit needed mid-flight.**
   Card parallelism failed partly because concurrent `git add`+commit from multiple forks race on the same git index.
   Raddle forks don't need this — each fork writes its own module doc to disk;
   **one combining commit** happens at the end (`fabric.SyncWeft(...)`, see `internal/fabricengine`), covering all raddle changes at once.
   This eliminates the git-index race entirely.
2. **Raddle only reads code, never writes it.**
   Card forks editing code concurrently risked seeing each other's unstable, half-finished intermediate states.
   Raddle forks read an already-landed, stable code state — no "who sees what when" problem.
3. **True file-disjointness is easy to guarantee.**
   With a clean module → doc mapping (one changed module → one raddle `.md` file), there's no ambiguity about who writes where, unlike card `changes-files` declarations which could turn out wrong after the fact.

**Structure:** parallel leaf forks (one per changed module, no dependencies between them) → one final step regenerating any top-level summary (`Overview.md`) from the now-updated module docs (must wait for all leaves) → one combined `fabric.SyncWeft(...)` commit covering everything.

**No race on `Overview.md`:** the "must wait for all leaves" sequencing above prevents concurrent writers to `Overview.md` within one regeneration run — it's a single, serial final step, never touched by the leaf forks themselves.
No additional lock needed there.

## When it runs: deferred to merge-time, not mid-task

Regenerating raddle is token-heavy and takes real wall-clock time, so it should run **once**, not twice.
Running it right after Webster (against the task's own fork-point) and then again at actual merge (against parent's real, possibly-since-moved HEAD) would do exactly that: two regenerations, the first thrown away the moment parent has advanced.

**Decision: raddle regenerates once, at merge-time, against parent's actual current HEAD** — not mid-task.
This collapses the two potential runs into one and guarantees the output describes the real merge result, not a stale fork-point.

**Consequence for the merge lock:** the lock protecting this step must span the **entire** critical section — read parent's current HEAD, run the leaf-fork + `Overview.md` regeneration against it, commit via `SyncWeft` — as one atomic unit, not just around the final git write.
If another task's merge landed in parent partway through regeneration, the docs would be stale against the HEAD they're about to be committed onto.
Same "advance only on confirmed success" discipline the `Warp-SHA` trailer mechanism uses elsewhere in `fabric` for recording a baseline, extended to cover the compute step, not just the write step.

**Decided:** raddle has no reserved phase slot of its own in loom's producer list (`contracts/recipes/loom-recipe.yaml`) — regeneration is folded into `Finalize`'s own contract instead, landed in `internal/landingshed`.
See internal/landingshed for Finalize's side of the contract.

## Staleness tracking, via `fabric`

Raddle's snapshot files describe the codebase as of some SHA, and only get regenerated by an explicit, separate command — they can silently drift out of date as cards land.
Using `fabric`'s Warp-SHA trailer mechanism (see `internal/fabricengine`):

- Raddle's regeneration command records its baseline by passing `snapshotTags=["raddle"]` to `Fabric.Commit`, alongside whatever raddle files the regeneration produced.
  **The warp SHA recorded should be the warp code SHA raddle describes — the last warp commit *before* the regeneration — not raddle's own resulting weft commit SHA**, otherwise later staleness checks compute against the wrong baseline;
  the `Warp-SHA` trailer holds exactly that value, so the trailer form satisfies this requirement naturally.
- A regeneration that finds the codebase unchanged since its last recorded baseline still needs to advance that baseline, even though it produces no weft content — this is exactly the case that motivated the empty-commit rule (see the tags-force-a-weft-commit Shared Decision in `internal/fabricengine`): tagging a `Commit` call with `snapshotTags=["raddle"]` and no changed files still lands an empty weft commit carrying the baseline, so a no-op regeneration advances the baseline instead of reporting drift forever.
- A staleness check is the **three-step** idiom `Fabric.SnapshotWarpSHA`'s own doc comment specifies, not the naive two-step composition: read the baseline via `SnapshotWarpSHA("raddle")`, confirm it still resolves via `f.Warp.SHAExists`, and only then call `f.Warp.ChangedFilesSince` to get a precise answer — *"raddle's map is N commits behind current HEAD, covering these files"* — instead of a vague, always-true warning that raddle "might" be outdated.
  Skipping the `SHAExists` check and calling `ChangedFilesSince` directly hard-errors on a warp SHA a rebase has since rewritten, exactly the case this mechanism exists to survive: the check lets a post-rebase raddle regenerate cleanly instead.

## Boundary with quarry (deliberately not coupled)

- **quarry** only cares about source code files, never markdown, and has **no knowledge of raddle whatsoever**.
- **Raddle never modifies code and therefore has no reason to notify quarry** — that coupling was proposed once during design and correctly rejected.
  Raddle's own use of `fabric` is purely for its own staleness tracking, unrelated to quarry.
- Both consumers independently depend on `fabric`;
  they do not depend on each other.

## What Master must know about raddle content (see `internal/websterengine`'s package documentation)

Raddle files are a **snapshot** of the codebase from *before* a plan started — they are only regenerated by a separate, explicit command, not continuously.
Master (and any fork inheriting its context) must treat raddle content as "how things were before this plan," never outranking a fresh quarry query or an actual file read once cards have started landing.

## Related

- `internal/fabricengine` — the `Warp-SHA`/`Snapshot` trailer and `SyncWeft` mechanics this design relies on.
- `contracts/recipes/loom-recipe.yaml` — the flat producer list Raddle has no slot of its own in;
  regeneration is folded into `Finalize`'s contract instead.
- The `internal/boardengine` package documentation — `PATTERN.md` (raddle's neighbor in `weft`) mentioned there.

entries.title: webster: worktree-per-card parallel execution
entries.brief: Give each DAG-independent group its own fabric-spawned worktree so concurrent cards stop sharing one git index; parked until measured evidence says it pays
entries.body:
From `manifest/roadmap.md` Someday.
Give each DAG-independent group its own `fabric`-spawned worktree, so concurrent cards stop sharing one git index.
A speed optimization over an already-correct sequential system.
The loom plan spec and `internal/websterengine`'s package documentation describe the sequential model it would extend.

## Design

> **Status: parked, not rejected — one shape was rejected, a second is open.** What two explorations rejected is *concurrent forks inside one working tree*, which race on a single shared git index; the 2026-08-20 worktree-per-group shape below does not share that index and is not covered by that rejection. Read past this banner before concluding the idea is dead — the earlier wording said "rejected for now both times" and, until the 2026-08-29 designs audit, sent readers away before the open shape, the measured case study, and the decision gate.
> Still parked, though one of its original three reasons has since fallen: the **Adopt quarry's glyph alphabet as the plan alphabet** item shipped (`go.mod` now requires `github.com/Knatte18/quarry`), so the DAG source this doc used to wait on exists. What still parks it: it is a speed optimization over an already-correct sequential system, and webster's landed card-list rewrite (`internal/websterengine`) should get real running mileage first. Reopen it on the measured evidence the Decision gate section names, never on estimate.
> Per the documentation lifecycle, if this is ever picked up the durable parts fold into `internal/websterengine`'s package doc and this file is deleted; if abandoned, this file is simply deleted.

## Why it's parked

loom-plan-spec.md is deliberately a flat, sequential card list with **no DAG wired into scheduling**.
Running cards as *parallel* forks would require reintroducing a DAG and worktree isolation, which reopens exactly the problem sequential execution avoids: git's index/staging area is a single shared file per working tree, so two forks concurrently committing — even to fully disjoint files — race on the same lock.
Current (2026) ecosystem guidance treats worktree isolation as effectively required for concurrent subagents on the same repo.
A declared-disjoint card pair that turns out (via deviation) to actually overlap is a **live corruption risk** in a concurrent-no-worktree model, not just a bookkeeping problem to fix after the fact as it is sequentially;
quarry would also see other forks' uncommitted, potentially syntactically-broken in-flight edits while serving a concurrent fork's query, since there's no filesystem isolation between them.

**A possible middle ground, if revisited:** let forks edit concurrently (the LLM-thinking-dominated part) but serialize the actual `git add`+commit+verify step through a mutex in webster's Go orchestration ("edit in parallel, land sequentially").
Even this requires *strictly enforced* file-disjointness (not just DAG-edge-absence) to be safe.
Not built.

## A possible unblocking shape (2026-08-20)

A structural alternative to the rejected concurrent-forks-in-one-tree shape above: each DAG-independent group (a batch, possibly one card) gets its own `fabric`-spawned worktree — genuinely its own git index/HEAD, which is what the rejected shape lacked — running the existing `Preflight → Webster → Finalize` row set unchanged, with `Webster`'s `Geometry.PlanDir` (already told, not derived) pointed at the source plan and a new batch-filter selecting the one group to run.
Merge-back reuses `fabric`'s existing merge machinery, not new infrastructure, and a group's completion gates on a build+test of the *merged* result rather than of the group's own worktree in isolation.
The ready set recomputes wave to wave rather than being precomputed upfront, so a group that turns out to depend on another's output is simply not ready yet instead of being mis-scheduled.

This shape is what makes the rejection at the top of this doc specific rather than general: that rejection was about concurrent forks sharing one checkout's git index, which worktree-per-group does not do.

Grouping granularity (one card vs. several) is orthogonal to safety — the original rejection above conflated it with the working-tree-sharing hazard, but genuine worktree-per-lane isolation is what actually matters.
Not yet a plan: the DAG source exists now that the **Adopt quarry's glyph alphabet as the plan alphabet** item has shipped,
but it still needs a writeup reconciling this with the still-open questions elsewhere in this doc (typical-plan wave-width evidence, the batchifier/planner change needed to emit groups).

The per-lane mechanics have since shipped elsewhere: batten's recipe (create, seed, run, teardown as ordinary producers) and its run-id addressing carry N concurrent lane runs side by side, so a lane is a batten-style run whose child seed names a webster-lane recipe — none of that machinery is this item's to build.
What remains genuinely webster's: the wave scheduler (event-driven, recomputing the ready set on each lane's merge-back — never a continuously maintained DAG), the plan group-filter, and a non-forking webster variant.
That last one is the real structural change: today's webster runs forks inside the Master session's own context, which binds execution to one session in one worktree;
a lane needs agents spawned into the lane worktree's own reed session instead, scoped to just that lane's group.

## The case study (from an earlier, more detailed design draft, `websterv2.md`, now retired)

A card-level dependency analysis of the 42-card plan that built webster v1 overturned the naive "linear chain" assumption:

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| Cards | 42 |
| Batches (sequential) | 9 |
| True card-DAG depth (critical path) | 7 |
| Peak wave width | 10 |
| Cards off the critical path | 83% (35 of 42) |
| Wave widths (1→7) | 10, 9, 7, 7, 6, 2, 1 |

- **The batch DAG over-constrains.**
  Sequential batching's own dependency declarations were largely spurious at card granularity — ~26 cards (waves 1–3) could have run as three parallel waves instead of spread across four sequential batches.
- **File-conflicts barely bind** when the plan is create-then-extend — nearly every file-conflict pair is already dependency-ordered into different waves.
- **The tail is the real ceiling, not dependencies** — a hard funnel near the end of a plan (e.g. final registration → sandbox validation) crashes wave widths regardless of fork budget;
  speedup is front-loaded.
- **Honest speedup estimate: ~2–3× wall-clock**, discounted from a naively-computed 3–5× because a wave's wall-clock is its *slowest* card,
  and the heaviest implementation cards tend to sit on the critical path.
  Two caveats push it down further: semantic edges were *inferred* from card descriptions (real edit-time dependencies only add edges and shrink waves), and 42 cards is an atypically large plan — a routine 5–10-card task has little fan-out headroom and would show a speedup near 1×, dominated by warm-context, not parallelism.

## Decision gate, if ever revisited

Run the card-DAG width analysis across several *real* completed plans, weighted for **typical** task size, not this one outlier.
Wide (fat waves, short critical path, low file-conflict) → an executor might pay off.
Narrow (long critical path, most cards chained, or simply few cards) → parallelism won't materialize;
sequential is the complete correct design, not just the MVP.

## The separable, cheap win already taken

A planner that emits true card dependencies (`depends-on`) instead of an over-constrained batch line recovers most of the *width* insight with **no worktrees and no concurrent execution** — this is exactly what loom-plan-spec.md already does.
Only the *executor that actually runs the width* (this entry) remains parked.

## Relationship to quarry (Part B of the retired draft)

The retired `websterv2.md` draft also had a Part B — structured impact lookup via `go/packages`/`gopls` (find-all-references as a Go verb instead of LLM-driven grep).
That idea is superseded, not lost: it's the direct ancestor of [quarry](https://github.com/Knatte18/quarry), which generalizes it to a multi-language, daemon-based design.

## Related

- `internal/websterengine`'s package documentation — the sequential model this would extend.
- loom-plan-spec.md — already captures the cheap win (`depends-on`).
- [quarry](https://github.com/Knatte18/quarry) — Part B's successor.

entries.title: reed: cross-worktree columns, own-window anchoring, per-window attach
entries.brief: Three related ideas for reed beyond one pane per strand and one window per worktree
entries.body:
From `manifest/roadmap.md` Someday, three items kept together:
- **reed: cross-worktree columns.** All worktrees in one tmux window, a column per worktree; needs a name for the new per-worktree grouping layer this introduces and a column-count/fallback policy.
- **reed: own-window strand anchoring.** A `display` anchor that spawns a strand into its own switchable tmux window instead of a pane.
- **reed: independent per-window attach via tmux session groups.** tmux's session-groups feature would let multiple `lyx reed attach` invocations show different windows independently, instead of sharing one today.

## Design

> Three related, not-yet-scoped ideas about reed outgrowing "one pane per strand, one window per worktree." Grouped here because each is a candidate building block for the others.

## Cross-worktree columns

All worktrees in one tmux window, a column per worktree.

Needs its own name for the per-worktree grouping layer this introduces — it cannot be called "session": that's already tmux's own term, and already 1:1 with a worktree in reed's plumbing today. Also needs a decision on how many columns fit before falling back to tmux windows-as-pages.

Candidate group-layer names surveyed so far and still free: **Heddle, Batten, Bobbin, Sley**. Already taken elsewhere in this codebase: Warp, Weft, Shuttle, Treadle, Shed, Loom, Reed, Strand, Fabric, Quarry, Crucible, and Selvage (claimed by the shipped header-replacement work — see `internal/reedengine`'s `selvagepane.go`).

## Own-window strand anchoring

A `display` anchor that spawns a strand into its own switchable tmux window instead of a pane.

## Independent per-window attach via tmux session groups

Today two `lyx reed attach` invocations join the same tmux session object — a shared "current window" pointer, and mismatched terminal sizes fighting over layout.

tmux's session-groups feature (`new-session -t <existing-session>`) would let each invocation show a different window independently, which reed's `attach` verb does not use today. This is a candidate building block for both ideas above, likely exposed as something like an `--window <n>` flag, or hidden entirely behind one verb that spawns the needed loose terminal windows automatically.

## Operator, 2026-10-05: strands in depth, not stacked in height

Two strands stacked as panes in one window are unreadable on a small laptop screen.
Stack them in depth instead: one tmux window per strand, behaving like tabs within the run's terminal window.

- The driver always lives in window 0, with its `loom-status` strand beside it.
- Each agent the driver spawns (Discussion-Write, a Burler round, Webster's Master) gets its own window, named by its role, so the tmux status line lists what runs.
- The window closes when the agent ends, and the view falls back to the driver.
- **No focus stealing.** A new window must never pull focus away from a window the operator is typing in; an automatic switch on spawn is unwanted for that reason.
  Open: how a new window announces itself instead (status-line highlight, tmux activity flag, a switch only when the current window is idle), and whether tmux session groups are needed so each attached terminal keeps its own current window.

entries.title: warp-visibility: CLAUDE.local.md invisible in the Fabric repo's git history
entries.brief: Expose CLAUDE.local.md by symlink so nothing lyx-related shows in the Fabric repo's history; the constraints half is out of date
entries.body:
From `manifest/roadmap.md` Someday.
Expose `CLAUDE.local.md` via symlink (Windows-Developer-Mode note and a copy fallback), so nothing lyx-related shows up in the Fabric repo's own git history.

Out of date as of 2026-10-04: the design below and the roadmap line say the `CONSTRAINTS.md`-equivalent half is covered because `PATTERN.md` lives in weft.
After `pattern-init`, `PATTERN.md` sits at the repo root and is tracked in the warp repo, so that half is not covered; decide it afresh when this is picked up.
The ignore entry for `CLAUDE.local.md` goes to `.git/info/exclude` through `fabricengine`, never a tracked `.gitignore` (the Fabric Git entry, `PATTERN-fabric-git`).

## Design

> **Status: Design — not built.** Split out from `internal/fabricengine` — the vacation-time discussion bundled this into the Fabric cutover step opportunistically ("we're touching that area anyway"), but the mechanism itself is filesystem-linking/worktree setup, not git coordination — it doesn't depend on `fabric`'s own architecture (`gitrepo`, `SyncWeft`, `RevertWithWeft`) at all. Per the documentation lifecycle, durable parts fold into whichever package ends up owning worktree setup (`warp`/`fabric`'s topology side, or `loom`'s init step) when this lands, and this file is deleted.
>
> **Scope reduced (2026-07):** the `CONSTRAINTS.md`-equivalent half of this task is superseded by the `PATTERN.md` item — `PATTERN.md` lives in `weft`, already invisible to the Fabric repo, so there is no constraints directory left to hide. This task now covers only `CLAUDE.local.md`.

## Design principle

Nothing lyx-related should be visible in the Fabric repo's own git history — everything lives in `weft`.

## `CONSTRAINTS.md`-equivalent — superseded by `PATTERN.md`

**No longer this task's concern.** `PATTERN.md` is the loomyard-owned `CONSTRAINTS.md`-equivalent,
and it lives in `weft` (see the `internal/boardengine` package documentation — "everything that isn't warp already lives in weft"), a separate repo reached through a junction into the warp worktree — so it is **already invisible to the Fabric repo's git history** simply by living there, with nothing extra to build.
This task therefore reduces to `CLAUDE.local.md` below.

## `CLAUDE.local.md` (a single file)

Loads alongside `CLAUDE.md`, additive.
Must physically exist in warp's working tree, so a directory junction doesn't apply directly:

- **Symlinks, not hard links.**
  Hard links are inode-based, not path-based — if whatever regenerates the source `CLAUDE.md` in weft uses the standard safe-write pattern (write to a temp file, atomic rename over the target), a hard link on the warp side keeps pointing at the *old* inode and silently stops reflecting updates.
  Symlinks are path-based and always resolve to whatever currently occupies the target path.
- **Windows note:** symlinks normally require admin, but Developer Mode (Settings → For Developers, Windows 10 1703+) grants `SeCreateSymbolicLinkPrivilege` to standard users without elevation — worth checking whether this can be enabled on managed/non-admin machines before assuming it's blocked.
- **Fallback if symlinks aren't available:** explicit re-link (or copy) at `loom` init time, not automatic filesystem-level linking.
  Accepts staleness only within a single run, not across runs — acceptable since `CLAUDE.md` content changes rarely mid-session.
- `CLAUDE.local.md` is **not** auto-gitignored by Claude Code — `loom`'s init step must explicitly ensure it's listed in warp's `.gitignore` (same mechanism already used for weft junctions).
- If warp already has its own pre-existing, committed `CLAUDE.md` (someone deliberately approved Claude's use in that repo), that's fine — `CLAUDE.local.md` loads alongside it and takes precedence on conflict, no special handling needed.

## Related

- The `internal/boardengine` package documentation and the shipped `PATTERN.md` — establish that `PATTERN.md`, the loomyard-owned `CONSTRAINTS.md`-equivalent, lives in `weft`, which supersedes this task's constraints-hiding half.
- `internal/fabricengine` — owned the junction re-pointing mechanism the now-superseded constraints-dir half would have reused (`CLAUDE.local.md` uses a symlink, not a junction).
- `internal/loomcli`'s session bootstrap — the init/session-bootstrap step that would trigger the symlink fallback and `.gitignore` entry for `CLAUDE.local.md`.

entries.title: Baseline producer and numerical-drift gate
entries.brief: Capture a before-state so a failure the task caused can be told from a pre-existing one; in numerical repos the failure to catch is drift
entries.body:
From `manifest/roadmap.md` Someday.
loomyard captures no before-state, so it cannot tell a pre-existing failure from one a task caused ([millhouse#1130](https://github.com/Knatte18/millhouse/issues/1130)).
In a numerical target repo (the drilling simulator) the failure to catch is drift, which an exit-code verdict like `plan.Verify`'s cannot express.

Agreed shape, not yet a design doc:
- A shared `Capture-Baseline` producer row right after `Preflight`, shared by reference the way `preflightshed` and `landingshed` share theirs, so the planner writes against the current numerical signature.
- The artifact lives in `.lyx/baseline/`, never `_lyx`: a numerical baseline is machine-bound (floating point, BLAS, compiler flags).
  Capture before the first edit, recompute after, compare, discard.
- Two seams, both owned by the target repo: `capture` (tree → artifact) and `compare` (before, after → verdict + findings, with per-channel tolerance).
  Loomyard owns the row, the seam shapes, and the artifact location.
- The gate rides `shuttleengine.GateSpec` on the `Webster` row; registering a validator name in `resolveGateSpec`'s switch is the unbuilt part.

Open:
- Whether compare runs once at Webster's exit (what `GateSpec` gives, since it fires at the Master run's finalize) or per batch (exact localization, a new batch-loop hook, N captures).
- A middle option: gate once, and localize by making the predicate of Webster's integration-stage `bisect` pluggable, at log₂(N) captures; bisect assumes monotone drift.
- A baseline tree whose capture itself fails should be recorded, not halt the run.

entries.brief: begin-batch refuses plan_drifted when an earlier batch already deleted a later card's Delete target
entries.body:
Seen 2026-10-03 in the `verify-publish-hardening` run, after 12 batches.
Batch 15 (card 15, `webster-verify-gate`) deleted `internal/websterengine/integration_test.go`, even though card 15 does not list it.
Card 17 lists the file under **Delete:**, so batch 16's `begin-batch` refused with `plan_drifted`: the path does not exist on disk and is not a Create target or Rename destination of any card.
The run blocked until the plan was edited by hand and rebaselined.

A Delete target that is already gone is the state the card wants, so it should not block the run.
Options:
- `begin-batch` accepts a missing **Delete:** path when an earlier batch's commit deleted it, and notes it in the batch record.
- The per-card check flags a batch that deletes a file outside its card, at the batch where it happens rather than at a later card.

entries.title: Webster schedules a Delete before its callers are removed
entries.brief: deriveEdges has no edge from a deleted symbol to the cards editing its callers
entries.body:
Seen 2026-10-03 in the `pair-lifecycle` run: Webster scheduled card 12 (`delete-half-removed-helpers`, which deletes `fabricengine.Topology.RemovePairBranch`, `PairBranchResult` and `PairSiblingRemnant`) before card 11, the card that removes their only production caller in `internal/battencli/wire.go`.
The batch then failed, with `recover-batch` refusing because the delete targets still resolve, and the run blocked at Webster.

`websterengine.deriveEdges` (`internal/websterengine/sequence.go`) orders card B after card A only when B's Uses names one of A's targets, or when A and B share a target and A has the lower number.
A card that deletes a symbol has no edge to the cards that edit its callers, because the callers appear in neither field.
Plan review did not catch the missing ordering either.

Possible fixes:
- Derive an edge from a Delete target to every card that edits a member referencing it, resolved through quarry.
- Have plan validation refuse a Delete whose symbol is still referenced from a member that a lower-numbered card edits, unless an edge already orders them.


From GitHub #350 (intake 2026-10-04).

entries.title: Webster begin-batch spends a minute validating the plan per batch
entries.brief: quarry#34 re-parses per target; fix it or validate incrementally; drop the per-batch model assertion
entries.body:
Seen on `test-suite-change-amplification` (2026-10-03), a 45-card plan that the Batchifier split into one card per batch.

## Measured

- `lyx webster validate` on that plan takes 64 s of wall time at 100 % of one core, with no child processes: the time is spent in-process, single-threaded.
- `begin-batch` runs `planglyph.ValidateDispatch` over the whole plan before every batch (`internal/websterengine/beginbatch.go:303`), so each batch pays roughly that cost again.
- The gap from one batch's report to the next batch's spawn was 143 s, 72 s and 81 s for the first three batches, while the forks themselves took 1–2 min each.
  Over 45 batches that is on the order of 50 minutes of setup.

## Cause

Not loomyard's own code: `quarry.Repo.Resolve` re-parses every file in a target's directory for each file target (Knatte18/quarry#34).

## Per-batch validation stays (operator)

Validating before every batch is deliberate.
A fork may drift from the plan when it finds something the plan missed, and the plan changes with it; the per-batch check is what notices.
It is also the base for running forks in parallel later: glyphs, quarry and the validator maintain, at every batch, a DAG that decides which cards and batches can run concurrently.

## Want

- quarry#34 fixed and the quarry dependency bumped, so one validation of a plan this size takes seconds.
- If that is not enough, make the per-batch validation incremental: re-resolve only the targets in files the last batch's delta touched, plus the cards that reference them, and reuse the rest from the previous batch.
- Drop `begin-batch`'s per-batch model assertion (operator): the fork inherits Merriam's model, so `begin-batch` has no model to check.

## Related

The one-card-per-batch split makes the per-batch cost dominate; whether the Batchifier should group cards more is a separate question.

entries.title: Webster audit and verify-gate halts are recoverable by the agent
entries.brief: Hung-shell gate wait, unacceptable contract-file findings, garbled way-forward text, recoveries that need denied commands
entries.body:
# Goal

A Webster run that halts on its run-exit audit or verify gate can always be recovered by the agent that receives the refusal, without the operator and without throwing away the run's batches.
These four notes stopped the `board-model` run on 2026-10-04.

# Decision (operator, 2026-10-05)

The global deny on `git reset --hard` stays.
Every reset a lyx refusal or stencil names is performed by lyx itself, in Go, guarded to the run's own task branch and a commit the run recorded (its start commit or a batch head), refusing on the parent's branch and on uncommitted changes that are not the run's own.
No refusal, stencil or spec (`contracts/specs/refusal-spec.md` included) may name a command the agents are denied.


# Decisions from the task discussion (operator, 2026-10-05)

- **Hung background shell.** The gate waits on a running background shell only up to a configurable bound; past it the turn counts as ended and the driver gets a message naming the shell.
  Subagent forks are still waited on as before.
  The deeper fix is that an agent never starts such a shell at all: find why Master ran `python3 -` reading stdin, and close that at its source (stencil or tooling).
- **No `python3` deny.** Loomyard must develop Python in other repos, whose tests run Python, so the agents' settings never deny it.
  What gets fixed is an agent reaching for Python where it did not need it.
- **Contract-file findings (hub's recommendation, not contested).** The verify gate's fixer stencil forbids writing `outcome.yaml` and `summary.md`,
  and accept-audit accepts a fork-contract-write finding once Master has rewritten those files in a later turn or they are absent.
- **Reset scope.** Whether the reset verb covers Webster only, or fabric's manual weft reset (`git -C <weft> reset --hard origin/<branch>`) as well, is left to Discussion: decide from what the refusals in each module need.
  The decision above on `git reset --hard` holds either way.

## Webster verify gate waits forever when Master ends its turn with a hung background shell

From note `webster-gate-hung-shell` (issues #361).

Imported from [issue #361](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/361).

Seen 2026-10-04 in `board-model`: after the verify gate re-prompted Master at 17:07:33, Master's fixer fork fixed the failure and Master's turn ended at 17:11, but the step logged nothing more for 75 minutes.
Master's Stop events (`.lyx/shuttle/<guid>/events.jsonl`) all carried `background_tasks` with a shell in state `running`: `python3 - 2>/dev/null; cat > /dev/null <<'EOF' … EOF; grep …`, where `python3 -` sat reading stdin forever.
The gate apparently does not count a Stop with a running background task as a turn end, so one hung shell blocks the run indefinitely; an operator prompt at 18:25 produced another such Stop and changed nothing.
Killing the `python3` process let the gate rerun verify at 18:26.

Expected: a turn end whose only running background task is a shell (not a fork) still counts, or the gate bounds the wait and surfaces "turn ended with background task X running" to the driver, which today cannot see or stop it (ly-drive has no verb for it, and Webster's interrupt policy is handback).
Also: lyx agents should not run `python3` at all (operator rule); the agent settings shuttle writes could deny it.

## accept-audit can never accept a fork-contract-write finding

From note `webster-accept-audit-contract` (issues #363, #365, #360).

Imported from [issue #363](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/363).

Seen 2026-10-04 in `board-model`: the run-exit audit flagged the verify-gate fixer fork for writing `_lyx/webster/outcome.yaml` (and `summary.md`), Master's contract files; Master had rewritten both afterwards.
`lyx webster accept-audit` refused even after HEAD was reset to the last batch head and both untracked files were deleted (their state at that head): "cannot be checked: …/_lyx/webster/outcome.yaml, …/summary.md; way forward: reset the branch to the run's start commit … and run lyx webster run --fresh".
`checkSuspectPaths` treats weft paths as unverifiable, so a `fork-contract-write` finding can never be accepted; the offered way forward throws away every batch (10 here).
The hub cleared `pendingAuditFindings` in `state.json` by hand to continue.

Expected: a contract-file finding is acceptable once the contract files are absent (Master rewrites them at its next terminal turn), or the gate fixer is kept from writing them in the first place.
Related: #361 (the same run's gate hang).


### From issue #365

Imported from [issue #365](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/365).

`lyx webster accept-audit` refused to accept pending audit findings:

```
webster: pending audit findings cannot be accepted: cannot be checked: _lyx/webster/outcome.yaml, _lyx/webster/summary.md; way forward: reset the branch to the run's start commit <sha> with git and run "lyx webster run --fresh"
```

Problems:

- The refusal says the two files "cannot be checked" but not why (missing, unreadable, changed since the audit, or not matching an expected state), so the caller cannot tell what to repair.
- The only way forward offered is resetting the branch to the run's start commit and rerunning with `--fresh`, which discards the run's work.
  There is no lighter path, such as regenerating the two files or re-running the audit.

Provenance: task `board-model`, note `webster-refusal-accept-audit.md`.

Imported from [issue #360](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/360).

## Webster run-exit audit: way-forward text ends mid-sentence and repeats paths

From note `webster-audit-way-forward-text` (issues #362).

Imported from [issue #362](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/362).

When the Webster run-exit audit halts a run as `blocked` on forged contract files, the way-forward text it prints is garbled.

The halt note reads:

> way forward: reset the branch to the run's start commit with git and run "lyx webster run --fresh" and re-step the Webster row (lyx webster run), since nothing the run recorded can check `_lyx/webster/summary.md`, `_lyx/webster/outcome.yaml`

The same two paths are also printed twice: once in each finding and again as "suspect paths".
The way forward also tells the operator to run `lyx webster run --fresh` and then `lyx webster run`, without saying whether the second command is a separate step or a restatement of the first.

Expected: a complete sentence stating why the forged files cannot be trusted, and an unambiguous ordered list of commands.

Provenance: task `board-model`, note `loom-halt.md`.

## No recovery path needs a command the agents are denied

From note `no-denied-recovery`.

Seen 2026-10-03 in the `pair-lifecycle` run: Webster refused a plan fix for a failed batch.
Its only named way forward was "reset the branch to the run's start commit with git and run `lyx webster run --fresh`" (see #350).
The driver, even in bypass mode, could not run `git reset --hard`, because `~/.claude/settings.json` denies `Bash(git reset --hard:*)` and a deny rule holds in every mode.
The run stopped until the operator ran the reset by hand.
`contracts/specs/refusal-spec.md` prescribes `git reset --hard <pre-fix head>` for another halt as well.

Idea (operator): a permission refusal must never stop the flow.
Every recovery a lyx refusal names must be doable by the agent that receives it.
Either lyx performs the destructive step itself, in Go, guarded to the run's own branch and start commit (`webster run --fresh` resetting the branch, a `keep|drop` verb for the integration fix commits), or the agents' permission set is loosened for what lyx's recoveries need.
Audit every refusal and stencil for commands the deny list blocks.
Related: `orch-live-hardening` (permission modes mean what they say).

entries.title: Orch context cycling and long-run hardening
entries.brief: Fresh reading after /compact, clear-or-compact as config, and the adopt/attach/permission hardening list
entries.body:
# Goal

`lyx orch` cycles its context correctly and runs for days without hand repair.
The stale reading after `/compact` and the clear-or-compact choice live in the same watcher code, and the hardening list touches the same adopt and context-reading paths.

# Decisions from the task discussion (operator, 2026-10-05)

- **Cycle mode.** `cycle_mode: clear|compact` in `orch.yaml`, default `compact`.
  A compact cycle keeps the session and its Remote Control link and passes the handoff instruction as `/compact`'s focus argument, so it writes no handoff file.
- **`permission_mode: prompt` is removed.** The orch never prompts for each action; `bypass` is the only mode, and the config key, its template comment and the orchengine doc say so.
- **Watchers.** `orch-no-watcher` is part of this task: the orch relies on driver and batten messages, and any gap they leave is closed in lyx code, never by a scratch watcher.
  Background shells and Monitors die with the process, which matters at adopt and reboot (a new `claude --resume` process), not at compact; Discussion verifies whether they survive `/clear`.


## Orch watcher cycles on a stale reading after /compact

From note `orch-compact-stale-reading`.

On 2026-10-04 the operator ran `/compact` in the orch session at 10:09:49Z.
It finished at 10:11:15Z (`compact_boundary`, trigger manual, preTokens 354815, postTokens 13673).
At 10:14:53Z the watcher sent the soft-cycle stencil and then cleared and resumed the session from a handoff, although the context held about 14k tokens.
`state.json` afterwards shows `cycle_trigger: soft`.

Cause: the watcher updates `LastContextTokens` only at a turn end (`internal/orchengine/watcher.go`, the `ContextTokens(ev)` call per turn-end event).
A `/compact` produces no turn end, so the reading stayed at the pre-compaction 354815, above `soft_threshold_tokens` (300000), and the soft trigger fired once `soft_idle_s` had passed.
`transcriptContextTokens` in `internal/shuttleengine/claudeengine/usage.go` would return the same stale number even if re-read, since it takes the last main-chain assistant entry's usage, which is still the pre-compaction one.

Expected: a manual compaction resets the reading, so the operator's `/compact` is not followed by a cycle.
Options: treat a `compact_boundary` entry newer than the last assistant entry as the reading (its `postTokens`), and re-read the transcript before firing a soft or hard trigger rather than trusting the stored turn-end reading.
The same applies to Claude Code's own auto-compaction (a residual named in `internal/orchengine/doc.go`).


From GitHub #356 (intake 2026-10-04).

## Orch cycle mode as config: clear or compact

From note `orch-cycle-compact`.

Seen 2026-10-03: the orch's context cycle uses `/clear` plus a handoff file, which starts a new conversation and may drop a Remote Control link the operator relies on from a phone.
Cycling through `/compact` keeps the same session, so Remote Control and session identity survive.
Idea (operator): the cycle mode as a config option, `clear` or `compact`; weigh what the handoff file gives that a compaction summary does not.

## lyx orch runs for days without hand repair

From note `orch-live-hardening`.

### Goal

The hub runs under `lyx orch` for days without hand repair: an adopt keeps the hub's watchers, the orch pane keeps its height, permission modes mean what they say, and a long transcript stays cheap to read.

### From the PR #337 review (2026-10-02)

- **Watchers after adopt.** The hub's background shells and Monitors die with the session it exits; `orch-template-adopt.md` does not tell the resumed session they are gone or to re-arm them.
- **Window size on attach.** With `window-size latest`, a `reed attach` from VS Code resizes the orch window to that client (seen on the PR #342 review, after #340's folderOpen fix landed).
- **`permission_mode: prompt`** adds no flag, so the session falls back to the user's `defaultMode` (`auto` here); the template comment and the orchengine doc promise prompts.
- **Smoke bypass check** proves nothing where `~/.claude/settings.json` allows `Bash`; assert the bypass footer or use a tool outside the allow list.
- **Large-session adopt** is untested: startup within `startup_timeout_s` and any resume dialog on a real hub transcript (decision record, open risk 2).
- **Stale context reading.** `ResetForFreshLaunch` keeps `LastContextTokens`, so `status` shows the previous session's reading until the first turn end after an adopt.
- **PID reuse** can refuse an adopt falsely; the registry's `procStart` tells a reused pid apart.
- **Transcript read cost.** `ContextTokens` reads the whole transcript on every idle turn end; read from the end.

## The orch relies on driver messages, not a scratch watcher

From note `orch-no-watcher`.

Seen 2026-10-03: the hub orch watches each driven run with a hand-written `.scratch/hub/watch.sh`, a background shell loop that polls the run's `status.json` every 30 s and exits on the first non-running state change.
It lives outside lyx, untested and uncommitted, and has to be re-armed by hand after every context cycle.
The driver already messages its parent (`ly:orch`) at every stop it cannot handle, which is the path the orch should rely on.
Idea (operator): question whether the orch needs a watcher at all; if a gap remains that the driver's message does not cover (a driver that dies without messaging, a stop the driver does not report), close it in lyx's own code, never with a scratch script.
Likely home: `lyx batten run`, whose Run-Shed row already polls the same `status.json` every 30 s.
Batten could message its parent on a non-running state change, and check the driver strand's liveness through reed to cover the case `internal/battenshed/doc.go` leaves out by design (a driver that dies, parks on a prompt, or stops with the run non-terminal).
Batten can also be started by hand from a terminal with no orch above it, so the parent is optional: message it when one is recorded, otherwise only log.

entries.title: Bouncer CIRCLING escalates to the parent; loomcli smoke tier green
entries.brief: CIRCLING judged later on unchanged recurrence and escalated to the parent orchestrator; fix the five failing loomcli smoke tests
entries.body:
# Goal

A Bouncer round loop does not halt a run for a human on something the parent orchestrator can settle, and the loomcli smoke tier is green on `main` before further loom runs depend on it.
`discussion-recurring-finding` and `circling-to-parent` are the same `board-model` halt seen from the anomaly report and from the Bouncer's verdict.

# Decisions from the task discussion (operator, 2026-10-05)

- **Checkpoint judging.** Below a checkpoint round the judge rules only `CONVERGED` or `CONTINUE`; it never rules `CIRCLING` there.
  At the checkpoint it decides whether more rounds are worth it: with progress it extends, never past `max_bounces`; with no progress (the same finding keys unchanged or reopened) it rules `CIRCLING`.
  A rising finding count alone is never circling.
- **Both numbers are configuration.** The checkpoint round (default 3) and `max_bounces` are configuration values;
  `max_bounces` lives in the recipe (`contracts/recipes/loom-recipe.yaml`) today, and Discussion settles where both live.
- **Escalation goes to the parent.** A `CIRCLING` ruling, and a budget spent without convergence, message the parent orchestrator the way a parent-review request does: a fork decides accept or continue and adds whatever design calls are needed.
  The operator is asked only when the parent cannot settle it, or the run has no parent.
- **The parent's decisions enter the decision record.** `post-discussion-additions` is part of this task: a verb records a parent's or operator's decision in the decision record, so plan review reads it as part of the answer key.
- **No GitHub issue for a recurring finding.** A recurring ledger finding goes to the parent as part of the circling escalation, not as a `selfreport` anomaly issue (#359 arrived with empty state and history).


## Discussion-Bouncer finding stays open across three rounds

From note `discussion-recurring-finding` (issues #359).

Imported from [issue #359](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/359).

### recurring-finding: a ledger finding stayed open across multiple rounds

**Slug:** board-model
**Parent:** main

**State:** 
**Current producer:** 

**Error:**
```

```

**History:**
no history entries

**Recurring finding:**
- Bouncer row: Discussion-Bouncer
- Ledger key: fold-target-semantics-open
- Rounds: [1 2 3]
- Status: open

## CIRCLING escalates to the parent orchestrator, later and on recurrence only

From note `circling-to-parent`.

Seen 2026-10-04 in `board-model`: Discussion-Bouncer judged round 2 CIRCLING because gating findings rose from 1 to 2, both in the D10 intake bound that round 1's fix had widened; the run halted for a human.
The hub settled it with five short design calls and the run went on; no operator input was needed.
Operator (2026-10-04): halting on that is disproportionate.
Idea: CIRCLING is judged no earlier than round 3 and only when the same finding keys recur unchanged, not on a rising count; and a CIRCLING verdict escalates to the parent orchestrator like a parent-review request (message, fork decides accept/continue with design calls), reaching the operator only when the parent cannot settle it.
Related: `post-discussion-additions` (a verb for the parent's decisions to enter the decision record, instead of the driver editing it by hand).

## loomcli smoke tier: five bootstrap/strand tests fail on main

From note `loomcli-smoke-failures`.

`go test -tags smoke ./internal/loomcli/` fails five tests on `main` (seen 2026-10-03 at `6a74ee1be`, during the PR-Gate review of #347, which fails the same five).
Each expects one `loom-status` or driver strand and finds none:

- `TestSmokeBootstrap_BringsUpSessionStrandAndDriver` — `smoke_test.go:530`: status strands named "loom-status" = 0; want exactly 1
- `TestSmokeBootstrap_SecondInvocationDoesNotSpawnASecondDriver` — `smoke_test.go:592`: status strands named "loom-status" after two bootstraps = 0; want exactly 1
- `TestSmokeDriverStrand_ReentrantAcrossThreeBootstraps` — `smoke_driverstrand_test.go:216`: driver strands after the first bootstrap = 0; want exactly 1
- `TestSmokeStep_LeavesAPreexistingStatusStrandUntouched` — `smoke_drivingsurface_test.go:100`: status strand guids after step = []; want exactly the one added before the step
- `TestSmokeStart_LLMRunRemovesEveryStatusStrand`

Either the smoke tests are stale against the current bootstrap, or bootstrap no longer brings up the status and driver strands it should.
Nothing runs the smoke tier in the normal verify, so the failures went unnoticed.


From GitHub #348 (intake 2026-10-04).

## Scope added after Discussion amends the decision record

From note `post-discussion-additions`.

Seen 2026-10-03 in `agent-self-reflect`: the operator added two scope items after Discussion had been approved, and the hub relayed them to the Plan-Write agent.
On the hub's instruction, Plan-Write put them in the plan overview as "operator additions", and plan review then removed them, because the plan must follow the decision record and the record did not carry them.
PR-Gate rejected the PR for the missing items, and the driver had to amend the decision record by hand before PR-Rework.

Idea (operator): a scope addition after Discussion amends the decision record, not the plan.
The agent that receives it (Plan-Write, or whoever holds the run) extends the discussion with the new decisions before planning on them, even if that is a little messy.
Possible shape: a lyx verb that appends an "operator addition" decision to the record and re-runs the mechanical discussion check, so plan review reads the addition as part of the answer key.

entries.title: Label descriptions, board CLI gaps, CLI tree exceptions
entries.brief: labels become label→description with lyx board labels; board get --body, merge --body-file, merged issues kept, slug limit in help; fix the five cliTreeFindings exceptions
entries.body:
# Goal

Board labels say what they cover, the board CLI does what the hub needs without hand-built JSON, and the CLI tree walk has no recorded exceptions left.

Labels principle (operator, 2026-10-05): labels exist only to group entries for merging into tasks; they name the lyx module an entry mainly touches, and an entry that belongs to no module carries none.

# Scope change (operator, 2026-10-05)

This task was narrowed while its Discussion was paused.
The skill and stencil work it first carried (ly-drive as a stencil, imperative skill loading) moved to task `lyx-skills-and-stencils`, which waits for two in-flight tasks that edit the same stencils.
The board CLI gaps below were added.
The `ly:board` skill stays; whether it is the only skill is no longer a goal of this task.

## Board labels carry a description of what each covers

From note `board-label-descriptions`.

Choosing the label is not always obvious from the name alone: landing (Describe, Publish, PR-Gate, Finalize) is part of `loom`, Discussion and Plan are `loom`, the batcher is `webster`, glyphs are `quarry`.
A YAML comment cannot carry that, since agents read the labels as a parsed list and `lyx config --set` rewrites the file.

- `labels` in `_lyx/config/board.yaml` becomes a map from label to a one-line description of what it covers.
  The type labels (`types`) get descriptions the same way; they are stored like other labels and only rendered differently.
- Validation keeps checking the keys only.
- A `lyx board labels` verb prints each label with its description.
- The `ly:board` skill tells the caller to read `lyx board labels` before choosing labels.

## Board CLI gaps the hub met on 2026-10-05

Merging notes into tasks forced the hub to extract and rebuild entry JSON with a script.

- `lyx board get` can print an entry's body alone, raw markdown, so a caller can edit it as a file.
- `lyx board merge` takes `--body-file` like `upsert`.
- A merge carries over the `issues` of the entries it removes onto the upserted entry, so GitHub provenance survives folding notes into a task.
- The help of every verb that takes a slug states the slug length limit (32 characters); the hub learned it from a refused intake import.

## Five CLI invariant exceptions in board notes, config, selfreport

From note `cli-tree-exceptions` (GitHub #349).

Part 2 of the test-suite cleanup (#347) added a CLI tree walk that checks every verb against the CLI invariant.
It records five exceptions in `cliTreeFindings` that pin existing behavior which breaks the invariant:

- `lyx board notes` (bare) and `lyx board notes bogus` print an extra "not initialized here" envelope.
- `lyx config` (bare) and `lyx config bogus` refuse with "not a git repository" before listing subcommands or refusing the unknown one.
- `lyx selfreport bogus` exits 0 and prints help instead of refusing the unknown subcommand.

Fix each verb and remove its entry from `cliTreeFindings`, so the walk enforces the invariant for it.

entries.title: ly-drive as a stencil, a ly:runs skill, and lyx-injected skill loading
entries.brief: Driver procedure moves into a stencil, a ly:runs workflow skill, and the orch watcher injects skill loading at start, adopt and after every cycle
entries.body:
# Goal

Every agent can drive lyx without rediscovering its workflows through `--help`, every role lyx spawns gets its procedure from a stencil, and no lyx session depends on an agent choosing to load a skill.

# Decisions (operator, 2026-10-05)

- **Skill or stencil.** A skill carries what any session needs to use lyx, the operator's own sessions and the orch included.
  A stencil carries one spawned role's procedure.
- **Skills are workflow guides, not references.** Cobra's `--help` stays the reference for flags and payload keys; a skill gives the concepts, the order of steps and one example per verb, like `ly:board`.
- **lyx injects skill loading; it never relies on a hook.** The scribe plugin's `SessionStart` hook asks a session to load `scribe:conversation` and `scribe:prose`, and on 2026-10-05 the orch saw the request and did not load either.
  A handoff skill would have the same weakness.

## The ly-drive skill becomes a stencil prompt

The `ly:ly-drive` skill exists only to start the drivers that run a loom through Shed with repeated `lyx shed step`.
Every other Claude process lyx spawns gets its instructions from a stencil prompt, and the driver should too.

- Move ly-drive's content into a stencil under `contracts/stencils/` and have the launch prompt render it.
- Remove the `ly-drive` skill from the `ly` plugin.
- `loom-bouncer-rounds` edits `plugins/ly/skills/ly-drive/SKILL.md` (its D6, the `parent_notice` to the parent); carry that edit into the stencil.

## A `ly:runs` skill for the run loop

The hub orch on 2026-10-05 had to find the loop through `--help`: what a skill should have told it.

- Spawn a task with `lyx batten run <slug>` from the prime, in the background; read progress with `lyx batten status`, and use `pause` and `goto`.
- A parent-review request arrives as a message naming a brief; a one-shot fork reads it, reviews and submits with the brief's `lyx loom review` command.
- Escalations from a child (CIRCLING, a spent review budget) arrive the same way, once `loom-bouncer-rounds` has landed.
- Landing and what the hub does after it, such as amending board entries a landed task superseded.
- Every lyx agent is reachable by name through Claude Code's `ListAgents` and `SendMessage`.
  Names follow `internal/agentname`'s fixed form: `<shortname>:<role>` in the prime, such as `ly:orch`, and `<shortname>:<slug>:<role>` in a task worktree, such as `ly:<slug>:driver` or `ly:<slug>:discussion`; reed injects a strand's own name as `LYX_STRAND_NAME` and its parent's as `LYX_PARENT`.
  So the orch can address any run's driver or writer directly, for a scope change or a resume, without going through the operator.
  Only `internal/agentname`'s doc states the form today; no skill or stencil tells an agent.
- Same shape as `ly:board`: concepts, steps, one example per verb, `--help` for the key set.

## The orch watcher injects skill loading at every entry

The orch prompt opens with an imperative to load `scribe:conversation`, `scribe:prose`, `ly:board` and `ly:runs` before anything else.
It reaches the session on every path in: `lyx orch start`, `--adopt`, and the resume after a cycle.
After a compact cycle the watcher types that prompt once the compaction has finished, since `/compact`'s focus argument only shapes the summary and the compaction drops the loaded skills' content.
`orch-cycle-hardening` rebuilds the cycle and the orch stencils; this builds on its result.

Settle which spawned roles also need the scribe skills: every role that writes prose for the operator or into the repo.

## Agents escalate to their parent, and act on the parent's answer

Seen repeatedly on 2026-10-05: a spawned agent (a Webster Master, a driver) stopped and asked the operator in its own pane instead of its parent, and an agent that did ask the parent then refused to act on the parent's answer and asked the operator again.
In `loom-bouncer-rounds` the Master asked the hub how to handle an environmental verify failure, got "cherry-pick 7ff4cfc1", and then asked the operator, citing that a message from another session cannot grant permission and that its stencil forbids it to run git.

Operator decision (2026-10-05): agents never stop to ask the operator; they ask their parent (`LYX_PARENT`), and the parent asks the operator only what it cannot settle.

- Every role stencil names its parent as the one to ask, by name, and says a question to the operator in the pane is never the way forward.
- Every role stencil says a message from its own parent (`LYX_PARENT`, under `internal/agentname`'s naming) is the operator's delegate and is acted on like an operator instruction, within the role's limits; Claude Code's default treats a cross-session message as an untrusted peer, and the stencil has to say otherwise.
- A parent's instruction that falls outside the role's limits (the Master may not run git) names who carries it out instead, so the parent never gives an instruction the recipient cannot follow; the parent's own guidance (`ly:runs`) says which role can do what.

entries.title: Webster Master hangs background shells with a flattened heredoc
entries.brief: cat > /tmp/x; python3 - <<EOF … EOF on one line reads stdin forever; seen twice on 2026-10-05 and in #361
entries.body:
Seen 2026-10-05 in two Webster Masters at once (`orch-cycle-hardening` and `webster-audit-recovery`), each with a background shell hung for about 80 minutes:

```
cd internal/shuttleengine/claudeengine && cat > /tmp/x 2>/dev/null; python3 - <<'EOF' 2>&1 | head -1 EOF echo ok
```

The heredoc arrived flattened onto one line, so `EOF` never closes it and `cat > /tmp/x` reads stdin forever.
It is the same shape as #361 in `board-model` (`python3 - 2>/dev/null; cat > /dev/null <<'EOF' … EOF`), so it is a recurring Master habit, not a one-off.
In `orch-cycle-hardening` it held the verify gate from 12:51 until the hub killed the `cat` at 12:56; the gate then ran verify.

`webster-audit-recovery` bounds the wait and gives every agent Bash call `/dev/null` as stdin, which ends the hang but not the habit.
Operator, 2026-10-05: an agent running Python like this is wrong; it needs a good reason to use Python at all (running a Python project's own tests is one), never as a stand-in for Read, Grep or Edit.
Open: why Master writes a multi-line heredoc that reaches the shell as one line, and why it reaches for `python3` and `/tmp` at all; the fix belongs in the Master stencil or the tool guidance it gets.

entries.title: A running verify gate is visible in status and on screen
entries.brief: After an agent ends its turn, a Go gate can run for minutes with nothing on screen; loom status and something on screen name the gate and its runtime
entries.body:
Seen 2026-10-05 in `orch-cycle-hardening`: after the Webster-Burler agent ended its turn, the producer ran the task's verify command (`verifyrun`: build, unit, integration, smoke vet) for many minutes.
Nothing on screen said so: the agent's pane sat idle, `lyx loom status` showed only `now=Webster-Burler`, and the operator read it as a hang, asked the agent what it was waiting on, and the agent could not tell either.

Idea (operator): a visible marker whenever a Go gate runs.

- `lyx loom status` (`activity.now`) names the gate and how long it has run, such as `Webster-Burler: verify running 6m (go test -tags integration)`.
- Something on screen shows the same: under the LLM driver every run uses, `lyx loom start` removes the `loom-status` strand on purpose (`internal/loomcli/start.go`, "the ly-drive strand is the driving surface"), so the marker goes in the driver's pane or title, the agent's title, or a status pane that also exists in LLM mode.
- The agent pane, or its strand's title, shows that the run moved on to a gate, so an idle agent does not look stuck.
- The same applies to every Go-side wait a producer does after its agent's turn: the Webster verify gate, the Burler round's verify, Publish's merge-in verify.

entries.title: fabric fetches an existing remote warp and weft branch instead of creating new ones
entries.brief: A branch that exists on origin is fetched and checked out, never recreated locally; reconcile and checkout today fork a fresh weft and fabric add refuses the warp
entries.body:
## Problem

Moving a running task to another machine needs a pair built from the task's existing warp and weft branches on origin.
Fabric handles an existing warp: `lyx fabric reconcile` adopts a warp worktree created outside lyx.
Finding the existing weft is the gap: `reconcile`, `checkout` and `add` probe only the local `refs/heads/<slug>-weft` (`weftBranchExists`).
When that ref is absent, `reconcile` forks a fresh dormant weft from the weft HEAD (`createDormantWeftForRawWarp`) and never looks at `origin/<slug>-weft`, so the run records and status are silently lost and the next push collides with origin.
Only `clone` adopts a weft branch from origin, and only for the prime.

## Workaround used on 2026-10-05

```
git -C <hub>/<repo>-weft branch --track <slug>-weft origin/<slug>-weft
git worktree add --track -b <slug> ../<slug> origin/<slug>
lyx fabric reconcile
```

With the local tracking weft branch in place, `reconcile` takes its `weft_recreated` path and wires junctions, portal and launchers.
`lyx batten run <slug>` from prime then resumed both the outer and the inner run, and the inner loom run continued from its producer row with a fresh agent.

The adopted pair's strands also lost their parent until the first weft write: see bug note `weft-lock-dir-drops-parent`.

## Proposal

When a branch exists on origin, fabric fetches it and checks it out as a tracking branch; it never creates a new local branch in its place.
`lyx fabric add <slug>` fetches `origin/<slug>` and `origin/<slug>-weft` when they exist, instead of refusing the warp branch as a diverged leftover.
Every other path that resolves a pair's weft branch (`reconcile`, `checkout`) checks `origin/<slug>-weft` the same way before forking a new one, as `clone` does.

entries.title: Tell runs and strands apart: tabs, pane titles and colors
entries.brief: Clickable run and strand tabs in two status lines plus pane-border titles, pinned by reed at boot; /color per strand role
entries.body:
## Problem

With a run live, the driver pane and the agents it spawns (Webster, Burler, Bouncer judge, Describe and the rest) look alike in tmux and in Claude Code, so it is often hard to see which session is which.

## Idea (operator, 2026-10-05)

Give each spawned session a color with Claude Code's `/color` command, so the driver stands apart from the agents it spawns.
Open question: one color per loom segment (Discussion, Plan, Webster, review, Describe, landing) rather than only driver against the rest; the operator would like that.

## Open

- Where the color is set: by the spawning code through reed when it starts the strand, or by the agent's own launch prompt.
- Whether the tmux pane border or status line should carry the same color, so the reed layout matches the sessions.


## Runs and strands as clickable tabs (tried live 2026-10-05, operator approved)

reed runs one tmux session per run on the hub's one server, each with one window named `claude`, so the default status line shows nothing to switch between.
The hub set these global options live on the reed server, and the operator wants reed to pin them at boot, like the `mouse` pin in `internal/reedengine/lifecycle.go`:

```
status 2
status-format[0] '#[align=left]#{S:#[range=session|#{session_id}]#{?#{==:#{session_name},#{client_session}},#[bg=yellow#,fg=black#,bold],#[bg=colour238#,fg=white]} #{session_name} #[norange default] }#[align=right]%H:%M '
status-format[1] '#[align=left]#{P:#[range=pane|#{pane_id}]#{?pane_active,#[bg=cyan#,fg=black#,bold],#[bg=colour236#,fg=white]} #{pane_index}:#{pane_title} #[norange default] }'
status-style bg=colour234,fg=white
pane-border-status top
pane-border-format ' #{?pane_active,#[bold],}#{pane_index}:#{pane_title} '
```

Line 1 lists every run (session) as a tab, line 2 the strands (panes) of the current run by role; a click switches through tmux's default `MouseDown1Status` binding (`switch-client -t =`).
Strand colors could later tint the pane tabs and borders per role.

entries.title: lyx webster reset covers the report-head and last-batch-head targets
entries.brief: Three Webster recovery sites and standalone mode still instruct git reset --keep; widen the reset verb so every recovery instruction names a lyx verb
entries.body:
## Background

`webster-audit-recovery` (PR #381) added `lyx webster reset --to start|pre-fix` so recovery never needs a denied `git reset --hard`.
Its plan recorded one deviation not covered by the decision record (D7): three sites still tell the agent to run `git reset --keep <sha>` rather than a lyx verb.
They move back to the report head or the last-batch head in record-batch, recover-batch and accept-audit (`internal/websterengine/gitwrap.go`), plus standalone mode.
The verb was not widened because its targets are only `start` and `pre-fix`.
`--keep` is not denied and refuses rather than discards, so it was accepted at PR-Gate.

## Proposal

Widen `lyx webster reset` with the report-head and last-batch-head targets, and point the three sites and standalone mode at it, so every Webster recovery instruction names a lyx verb.

entries.title: A weft worktree without .weft/ silently drops LYX_PARENT from every strand
entries.brief: ReadOriginFor answers no record when the untracked .weft lock dir is missing, so a pair recreated by reconcile launches strands with no parent and no warning
entries.body:
## Bug

A strand launched in a pair whose weft worktree lacks the untracked `.weft/` lock directory gets no `LYX_PARENT`, silently.
`hubgeom.ResolveParent` reads the pair's origin record through `fabricengine.ReadOriginFor`, which requires both `_lyx/fabric/origin.json` and `.weft/`, and answers "no record" when either is missing.
`ResolveParent` then returns no parent, `hubgeom.reedGeometry` exports none, and nothing warns.

## Seen 2026-10-05

After moving `loom-bouncer-rounds` from another machine, its weft worktree was recreated by `lyx fabric reconcile` from the existing branch, which does not create `.weft/` (`lyx fabric add` does).
The driver, launched at 15:36:00, had no `LYX_PARENT`; `.weft/` appeared at 15:36:19 with the first weft write, and the Burler launched at 15:58 carries `LYX_PARENT='ly:orch'`.
The driver therefore could not reach its parent orchestrator.

## Fix

- Every path that creates or recreates a weft worktree creates `.weft/` (`reconcile`'s `weft_recreated` path at least).
- A present origin record with a missing lock directory is an error or a warning naming the gap, never a silent "no parent".

entries.title: lyx files bug issues from Go code; only reflection agents should
entries.brief: Tier 1 anomaly issues carry only keys and blank fields; drop Go-side filing and feed anomalies to Friction-Reflect instead
entries.body:
lyx's Go code must not file bug reports itself.
Self-reported bugs are written by an LLM agent through reflection (the Tier 2 `Friction-Reflect` producer), which can say what went wrong, why it matters and what to do.

Tier 1 (`internal/loomengine/anomaly.go`, `internal/loomcli/selfreport.go`, from `095cfa5b6`) files a GitHub issue per Go-detected structural anomaly, and those issues say nothing.
Issues #366–#382 from 2026-10-05 show it:

- A recurring-finding issue (e.g. #370) carries only the ledger key (`d4-budget-test-off-by-one`), the Bouncer row and the round numbers, not the finding, the reasoning or how it ended.
- State, current producer and error print blank, and history prints "no history entries", even when the run had them.
- Crash-resume issues (#376–#380) fired for the deliberate migration of four runs between machines.
- Every issue gets the `bug` label, though a recurring finding or a spent budget is a process signal, not a defect.

The hub set `selfreport: false` in main-weft's `_lyx/config/loom.yaml` on 2026-10-05 to stop the filing.

Proposal:

- Remove Tier 1's GitHub filing and the `selfreport` config key.
- Keep the Go detection, and pass the detected anomalies to `Friction-Reflect` as input, so the reflection agent decides whether any of them is worth an issue and writes it with its content: what happened, why it is abnormal, what to do.
- Treat a deliberate resume (adopt, takeover, `lyx loom start` after a migration) as no anomaly.

entries.title: Measure and prune the test suite
entries.brief: Stage 2: per-test coverage tool, delete redundant tests, seam real-time waits, parallelize fabricengine, stop the tmux socket leak, budget guard
entries.body:
Stage 2 of getting the test suite under control: measure it, then cut it down.
It runs after `test-writing-rules`, so its own changes follow the new rules, and runs alone: it touches test files in nearly every package.

The suite grew from 1967 test functions on 2026-08-13 to 5749 on 2026-10-05, and the integration tier from 17.9 s to 57.5 s on the same idle machine.
The two test revisions of 2026-10-03 (`22e46970e`, `5805c58fb`) removed duplicated helpers and hardcoded expectations, but left the count unchanged.

## Measure

- Build a tool (e.g. `cmd/testprune`) that runs per-test coverage and lists tests with no unique coverage: every line they cover is covered by another test.
  It reports per package: test count, wall time, serial time, and the redundant candidates.
- Record the before-state in `docs/benchmarks/test-suite-timing.md` with its slowest-tests table.

## Clean

Package by package, largest first (`internal/fabricengine`, `internal/websterengine`, `internal/reedengine`, `internal/shuttleengine`, `internal/loomcli`, `internal/shedadapters`, then the rest):

- Delete the tests the tool reports as redundant, after checking each one does not pin a contract the coverage view misses (an error message, an output shape).
- Fold near-identical tests into table-driven tests.
- Move integration tests that need neither git, tmux nor processes to the untagged tier with `internal/testkit` fakes.

## Speed

- Give real-time waits a test seam: the reed watchdog discovery interval (`watchdog.go`), `reapExitTimeout` (`reedengine/lifecycle.go`), verifyrun's `waitDelay` (`verifyrun/run.go`); use `true` instead of `sleep 5` in `verifytree/verify_integration_test.go`.
- Add `t.Parallel` to fabricengine's serial integration files where tests are independent (`mergein_recovery_integration_test.go`, `commit_integration_test.go`, `pull_integration_test.go`, `warpbinding_clone_integration_test.go` and others; 425 of 698 tests run serially).
- In `bareVocabularyTokenIn` (`lyxcwd/enforcement_test.go`), skip the regex when the lowercased text contains neither "weft" nor "warp".
- Arm the hermetic git env in `gitrepo/internal/gitoracle`.

## Socket leak (from note `tmux-socket-leak`)

Test runs leave dead tmux socket files in `/tmp/tmux-1000/`: 659 on 2026-10-05, and every suite run adds more.
Prefixes, most to least common: `lyx-warp-bare-LYXHUB-*` (over 400), `lyx-001-*` (standalone geometry, `internal/standalonegeom/reedgeom.go` `SocketKey`), `lyx-contract-*-test-<pid>-<n>` (`internal/reedengine/contract_integration_test.go`), `lyx-dotfill-harness-*`, `lyx-attach-harness-<pid>` (`internal/reedcli/smoke_attach_test.go`), `lyx-<hash8>`, `lyx-Test*`.

- `kill-server` stops a server but leaves its socket file: remove the socket in test cleanup through one shared helper (see `pattern/PATTERN-tmux-test-isolation.md`), and point `TMUX_TMPDIR` at `t.TempDir()` where possible so the files never reach `/tmp`.
- Check whether production reed paths (standalone geometry, warp-bare) also leave sockets.
- A full suite run leaves no new file in `/tmp/tmux-$UID/`.

## Consolidate PATTERN's Testing section

`test-writing-rules` added three Testing entries (`PATTERN-test-economy`, `PATTERN-test-time-seam`, `PATTERN-test-parallel`); the operator wants the section revised, not grown.
Proposal to settle in Discussion: merge `test-tier-purity`, `test-time-seam` and `test-parallel` into one `PATTERN-test-speed`, and `hermetic-git-tests` and `tmux-test-isolation` into one `PATTERN-test-isolation`, leaving Testing with test-economy, test-speed, test-isolation, testkit and hubforge-fixtures.
Enforcement tests that name the old entries move with them.

## Budget guard

Once the suite is pruned, a guard test pins a per-package budget for test count and wall time at the after-state; exceeding it fails until the budget is raised deliberately in the same commit.

## Done when

- The after-state is recorded beside the before-state in the benchmark doc.
- The test count and the integration tier's wall time have dropped substantially; the task's PR states both numbers.
- Coverage of non-test code has not dropped beyond what deleted redundant tests explain.

entries.title: Test-writing rules that stop the suite regrowing
entries.brief: Stage 1: tests per behavior not per symbol, no redundant tests, redundant tests are review findings
entries.body:
Stage 1 of getting the test suite under control: change how tasks write tests, so that no later task, `test-suite-prune` included, adds tests by the old habit.

Today's contracts drive one test per symbol: `contracts/specs/loom-plan-spec.md` and `contracts/stencils/loom/loom-template-plan.md` say every card that introduces behavior bundles its own test, and every independently testable symbol gets its own card.
Nothing asks whether a new test covers anything not already covered.

- Tests target behavior and contract at a module's public surface, not each helper.
- A new test must cover something no existing test covers; otherwise it extends an existing table test.
- A review fix adds a test only when the finding is a coverage gap; otherwise it corrects an existing test.
- The Bouncer and Burler rubrics treat a redundant test as a finding, like a missing one.
- The card-granularity rule changes with the test rule: cards and their tests follow behavior, not symbols.
- Audit `PATTERN.md` and `pattern/` for rules that demand a test per item (e.g. `PATTERN-refusal-way-forward`'s reaching test per refusal) and let one table-driven or contract-level test cover many items; add a Testing-section PATTERN entry for the new rule.
- Check whether `scribe:testing` (separate repo `~/Code/scribe`) needs the same change; name it, do not edit it.
